problems.note: Story card 5 says 'So each gets 1 and 1/3' and the screen shows '4 ÷ 3 = 1 1/3'. Text-to-speech may read '1/3' as 'one slash three', which a child who can't read can't follow. Spell the fraction out in words in the spoken text, e.g. 'one and one third'.
The narration and choices ('1 1/2', '1 1/3') are fraction numerals, which are hard to follow by ear. Speak them as words ('one and a half', 'one and one third'). The marked answer (1 1/3) is correct.

The choices '2 1/2' and '2 1/3' are only distinguishable by the spoken fraction. Read them aloud as 'two and a half' and 'two and one third' so a child listening can tell them apart. The marked answer (2 1/2) is correct.
Choices '3 1/3', '3 2/3' and '3' are hard to tell apart by ear when spoken as numerals. Use spoken words, e.g. 'three and one third'. The marked answer (3 1/3) is correct.
Four similar fraction choices (1 1/6, 1 1/3, 1 2/3, 2) are very hard to tell apart by ear. Speak them as words. The marked answer 1 2/3 is correct (10 ÷ 6 = 1 remainder 4, and 4/6 = 2/3).

The Why explanation skips a step. It says 'Four are left. Cut each into 3 pieces. Each friend gets 1 and 2/3,' but it never shows that 12 pieces shared by 6 friends gives 2 pieces each, which is 2/3. Add that step so the reasoning is complete.

The marked answer 'yes' is correct: 7 ÷ 4 = 1 3/4. Two things to consider. First, the item is a yes/no guess with only two choices, so it is weaker practice than the others. Second, fourths of a leftover with a mixed number is at the top edge of Grade 2 content. Consider a more demanding question, or a version with a wrong fraction such as '1 1/4' as the distractor, so the child has to work out the answer.
